introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et quelques espaces sont manquants à l'impression (question 8 : « between1871and1890 », rétabli en « between 1871 and 1890 ») ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante (dates, traités) ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 4 : l'énoncé imprimé date le déclenchement de la révolte Mau Mau de 1951. L'historiographie situe la montée de la violence en 1950-52 (mouvement interdit en août 1950, état d'urgence proclamé le 20 octobre 1952) ; le sujet est recopié tel quel et le corrigé précise la chronologie sans corriger l'énoncé.

Question 5 : l'Afrique équatoriale française regroupe le Gabon, le Moyen-Congo, l'Oubangui-Chari et le Tchad ; le Cameroun, ancien mandat puis tutelle, n'en faisait pas partie. Les interventions militaires françaises (Gabon 1964, Tchad à partir de la fin des années 1960, Centrafrique 1979) et le rôle du réseau Foccart sont cités selon l'historiographie courante, sans chiffres.

Question 7 : le sujet emploie « romanisation » au sens de la promotion du catholicisme romain par Jacques II ; les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, acquittement des sept évêques et invitation à Guillaume le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre).

Question 9 : le montant des réparations (132 milliards de marks-or, fixé en 1921) et les pertes territoriales sont cités de mémoire historique établie ; aucune statistique de population n'est avancée.

Question 11 : la Banque mondiale et le FMI sont des institutions spécialisées de l'ONU ; l'UNICEF (fonds et non institution spécialisée) n'est volontairement pas traité. Les dates (variole déclarée éradiquée en 1980, Alma-Ata 1978, convention 182 de l'OIT en 1999, Codex Alimentarius 1963, retrait des États-Unis de l'UNESCO en 1984-85) sont citées selon l'historiographie courante.

Question 12 : le sujet vise la rupture sino-soviétique après la mort de Staline (1953). Les dates (discours de Khrouchtchev en février 1956, rupture de l'accord nucléaire en 1959, retrait des conseillers en 1960, congrès de Bucarest en juin 1960, guerre sino-indienne 1962, incidents de l'Oussouri en mars 1969) sont données selon l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre n'est avancé.

Thèmes : les noms sont qualifiés pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone (`sino-soviet split`, `afrikaner nationalism`, `mau mau revolt in kenya`...) ; plusieurs sont réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2021 (`scramble for africa`, `apartheid in south africa`, `cold war`, `indirect rule in colonial africa`) ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
How far were political and humanitarian factors responsible for the European scramble for Africa in the late 19th century?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The scramble for Africa was the rapid partition of the continent by European powers, roughly between the 1880s and 1900; in about twenty years almost the whole of Africa, except Ethiopia and Liberia, came under European control. Historians explain it by a combination of economic, political, strategic and humanitarian causes. The question asks how far political factors (power rivalry, prestige, strategic needs) and humanitarian factors (ending the slave trade, spreading Christianity and "civilisation") were responsible. The argument here is that political factors were the most important and the humanitarian ones were real but mainly served as a justification, with economic motives and technology acting as important conditions.

**1. Political factors.**
- *Great-power rivalry and the balance of power.* After German unification (1871) and the Franco-Prussian War, European states competed for status. For France, which had lost Alsace-Lorraine, colonies were a way of recovering prestige. Britain wished to protect its position as the leading world power. A new colonial claim by one power often provoked a rival claim, so that the process fed on itself.
- *Germany's entry.* Bismarck, who had been reluctant to acquire colonies, claimed Togoland, Cameroon, South West Africa and East Africa in 1884-85 partly to please German commercial and nationalist opinion and to use colonial disputes in his diplomacy. In Cameroon Gustav Nachtigal made treaties with the Duala chiefs in July 1884, only days before the British consul arrived.
- *Strategic considerations.* The Suez Canal (opened in 1869) made Egypt a vital route to India; the British occupation of Egypt in 1882 pushed Britain to secure the Nile valley and the Sudan, and to hold the Cape route, while France competed with Britain in West Africa and on the Nile (the Fashoda incident of 1898).
- *Leopold II and the Congo.* Leopold II of Belgium, who set up the International African Association (1876) and employed Stanley, forced other powers to respond to his claim, which led to the Berlin West Africa Conference of 1884-85.
- *The Berlin Conference and the rule of "effective occupation".* The conference regulated claims to the African coast (a European power had to occupy effectively), which produced a race to sign treaties and place garrisons inland.
- *Domestic politics and national prestige.* Colonial success was seen as a way to win popular support and to distract attention from social tension at home.

**2. Humanitarian factors.**
- Public opinion had been shaped by explorers and missionaries, above all David Livingstone, whose call for "Christianity, commerce and civilisation" was meant to replace the slave trade with legitimate trade.
- The East African slave trade continued and was exposed by missionaries and explorers. Cardinal Lavigerie campaigned in Europe against it in 1888-89, and the Brussels Anti-Slavery Conference of 1889-90 committed the powers to suppress it. The General Act of Berlin (1885) also declared a commitment to end slave trading and to protect missionaries and native populations.
- Missionary societies pressed governments to protect their stations and converts, which sometimes led to the extension of political control.
- However, humanitarian arguments were often used to justify actions already decided on other grounds. Leopold's "philanthropic" project in the Congo became one of the most brutal systems of exploitation, which shows how far this language could hide political and economic aims.

**3. Other factors.** Economic motives (the search for raw materials and markets during the depression of the 1870s and 1880s, and for investment outlets) mattered, but the profits from tropical Africa were not as large at the start as the explanation suggests. Technology (quinine against malaria, steamships, railways, the machine gun) made conquest possible, and African political divisions and rivalries allowed Europeans to play off one group against another.

**Evaluation and conclusion.** Political rivalry and fear of losing out to rivals were the main reasons why the partition took place so fast and in the form that it did. Humanitarian ideas were an important background, sincere for many missionaries and campaigners, but they did not by themselves cause governments to take over territory; at most they gave moral cover and public support. Therefore political factors were responsible to a very large extent, and humanitarian factors only to a limited extent, working with economic and technological causes.
